items.title: Privacy & informatiebeveiliging: dit speelt er in de bibliotheek
items.raw_text: Privacy en informatiebeveiliging zijn belangrijke onderwerpen voor iedere bibliotheek. Maar wat betekenen nieuwe ontwikkelingen nu concreet voor de praktijk? Vanaf nu delen we iedere twee maanden de belangrijkste ontwikkelingen, praktische tips en aandachtspunten voor de bibliotheeksector. items.title: Voorlezen in de taal van je hart: meer verhalen in Farsi en Papiamentu
items.raw_text: Een Curaçaos meisje dat glundert als ze het boek ‘Mihó nò’ ontdekt tussen de bibliotheekboeken. Een Iranese vader die een bibliotheekmedewerker speciaal komt bedanken, omdat hij een prentenboek in zijn thuistaal mee kan nemen. Of een Farsi-sprekende moeder die ontroerd raakt, als ze tijdens een bijeenkomst hoort dat dromen en schelden in je thuistaal normaal is. items.title: Haal meer uit data voor maatschappelijke programmering met de Datateam®methode
items.raw_text: Hoe maak je keuzes rond programmering die niet alleen goed voelen, maar ook goed onderbouwd zijn? Die vraag stond centraal tijdens de inspirerende en energieke workshop Haal meer uit data – De Datateam®methode op 4 juni bij Kunstwerk! in Zevenaar. Dertien bibliotheekmedewerkers uit Gelderland en Overijssel maakten kennis met de Datateam®methode. Universiteit Twente ontwikkelde deze aanpak, die organisaties helpt om maatschappelijke vraagstukken data-geïnformeerd aan te pakken. Van vraagstuk naar inzicht Tijdens de interactieve workshop wisselden theorie en praktijk elkaar af. Deelnemers gingen aan de slag met vraagstukken uit hun eigen organisatie. items.title: HR Actueel – Mogelijke afschaffing compensatie transitievergoeding: wat betekent dit voor bibliotheken?
items.raw_text: Vanaf 2027 ontvangen werkgevers mogelijk geen compensatie meer voor de transitievergoeding bij ontslag wegens langdurige arbeidsongeschiktheid. Dat heeft het kabinet aangekondigd. Hoewel de parlementaire behandeling nog loopt, is het voor bibliotheken en cultuurorganisaties verstandig om nu alvast inzicht te krijgen in de mogelijke gevolgen. Extra kosten bij langdurig verzuim Langdurig verzuim brengt al aanzienlijke kosten met zich mee. Denk aan twee jaar loondoorbetaling, re-integratietrajecten, arbodienstverlening en vervanging van medewerkers. Als de compensatieregeling verdwijnt, komen daar mogelijk ook de kosten van de transitievergoeding volledig bij. De financiële impact kan aanzienlijk zijn. Een medewerker met twintig dienstjaren en een bruto maandsalaris van € 3.500 heeft bijvoorbeeld recht op een transitievergoeding van ruim € 23.000. Zonder compensatie zijn deze kosten volledig voor rekening van de werkgever. Daarmee wordt langdurig verzuim niet alleen een HR-vraagstuk, maar ook een belangrijk onderwerp voor directie, management, begroting en risicomanagement. Aandacht voor slapende dienstverbanden Ook de discussie rondom slapende dienstverbanden kan opnieuw relevanter worden. De compensatieregeling werd destijds ingevoerd om te voorkomen dat werkgevers dienstverbanden na twee jaar ziekte lieten doorlopen om betaling van de transitievergoeding te vermijden. items.title: De tanden in een meerjarenplan
items.raw_text: Elke bibliotheek of MFCO maakt ze: meerjarenbeleidsplannen. Sommigen verheugen zich erop om ermee aan de slag te gaan, anderen vinden het nog best ingewikkeld. Wat moet er precies in? Wat is een goede doelstelling en wie moet je allemaal betrekken? En wat is het verschil tussen een meerjarenbeleidsplan van de bibliotheek en een meerjarenplan van de gemeente in het kader van de zorgplicht? Elk jaar ondersteunt Rijnbrink een flink aantal organisaties in dit proces. Met plezier en met resultaat. De afgelopen periode zetten we samen met de bibliotheek Noord-Veluwe , de bibliotheek Dalfsen en BIJ de bieb de tanden in hun meerjarenplan. In dit artikel lees je hun ervaringen. Bijzonder was dat, naast alle medewerkers, ook de beleidsambtenaar het hele traject heeft meegedaan. Ook waren er verschillende afstemmingsmomenten met samenwerkingspartners. Dat leverde veel lof op. De bibliotheek voegde aan het plan gelijk een paragraaf toe over alle onderdelen die de gemeente mee moet nemen voor de zorgplicht. items.title: ‘Veranderen doe je via consensus én met fermheid’
items.raw_text: Binnen Digitaal Doordacht onderzoeken we hoe digitalisering in de publieke sector daadwerkelijk bijdraagt aan betere dienstverlening, meer openheid en groter vertrouwen. Het veranderverhaal van Jolein Baidenmann laat zien dat echte openheid niet draait om simpelweg méér informatie openbaar maken, maar om informatie die voor mensen daadwerkelijk begrijpelijk en bruikbaar is. Wat haar aanpak bijzonder maakt, is hoe zij in een complexe publieke omgeving beweging creëert: door belangen zichtbaar te maken, partijen te verbinden en draagvlak te combineren met duidelijke keuzes. “Soms moet je als leider keuzes maken en stevig zijn: ik heb iedereen gehoord, maar we gaan toch die kant op.” Jolein Baidenmann is verandermanager en werkt met die insteek aan een overheid die openheid op een betekenisvolle manier probeert waar te maken. “Het is belangrijk dat een open overheid de samenleving in staat stelt om mee te denken, te controleren en gebruik te maken van de informatie die bij de overheid beschikbaar is.” Als manager Open Overheid en plaatsvervangend directeur Open Overheid bij het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) is Baidenmann bij uitstek de persoon om het concept ‘open overheid’ in praktijk te brengen. items.title: Juli
items.raw_text: Online radicalisering van jongeren: het gesprek gaat door Deze maand is er opnieuw veel aandacht voor schadelijke en gewelddadige online netwerken. De NOS berichtte op 23 juli over de aanhouding van een jonge man die wordt verdacht van deelname aan een sadistisch Com-netwerk ofwel community. Binnen dergelijke besloten online groepen kunnen kwetsbare jongeren worden geronseld en aangezet tot zelfbeschadiging, misbruik en geweld. De actuele berichtgeving raakt direct aan de onderwerpen die op 22 juni centraal stonden tijdens het symposium Online radicalisering van jongeren: herkennen, begrijpen en handelen, georganiseerd door de ATKM, de NCTV en ECP. Onder leiding van dagvoorzitter Liesbeth Rasker gingen professionals, onderzoekers en ervaringsdeskundigen in gesprek over de vraag hoe online radicalisering tijdig kan worden herkend, zonder jongeren te snel te veroordelen of te stigmatiseren. Radicalisering begint vaak niet met een uitgesproken ideologie of een duidelijke intentie om geweld te gebruiken. Het kan beginnen bij menselijke vragen: wie ben ik, waar hoor ik bij en wie neemt mij serieus? Online groepen kunnen daarop inspelen en grenzen tussen humor, provocatie, uitsluiting en geweld geleidelijk laten vervagen. De rode draad in het symposium, de podcast en de actuele berichtgeving is daarom dezelfde: blijf nieuwsgierig, investeer in kennis van de online leefwereld en voer het gesprek voordat standpunten en gedrag verder verharden. items.title: Zomerblog Marjolijn Bonthuis
items.raw_text: “Worden we een museum?” Een persoonlijke zomerse beschouwing over Europa, AI en de stap van dialoog naar daadkracht Deze zomer lees ik Grand Hotel Europa van Ilja Leonard Pfeijffer. Het hotel in de roman staat symbool voor Europa: prachtig, rijk aan verhalen, maar vooral gericht op het verleden. Europa bewaart zijn kunst, architectuur en geschiedenis — en verkoopt die aan toeristen. Ondertussen wordt de toekomst elders gebouwd. Die gedachte dringt zich ook op wanneer ik kijk naar de huidige technologische ontwikkelingen. Terwijl Amerikaanse en Chinese bedrijven miljarden investeren in kunstmatige intelligentie, chips en digitale infrastructuur, zijn wij in Europa vaak vooral bezig met regels, risico’s en bescherming. Laat ik daar duidelijk over zijn: die aandacht is nodig. Zeker vanuit mijn dagelijkse verantwoordelijkheid voor digitale veiligheid, weerbaarheid en vertrouwen weet ik hoe belangrijk het is dat technologie niet zonder grenzen wordt ontwikkeld en toegepast. Big Tech heeft inmiddels zoveel economische, technologische en maatschappelijke macht opgebouwd dat stevige publieke kaders onvermijdelijk zijn. Bescherming van grondrechten, democratische controle en eerlijke concurrentie zijn geen luxe. Maar regels alleen maken ons nog geen speler. Als Europa vooral vastlegt onder welke voorwaarden technologie van anderen hier mag worden gebruikt, terwijl we zelf onvoldoende investeren in de ontwikkeling ervan, blijft onze invloed beperkt. items.title: Stichting ECP wijzigt structuur governance om ook in de toekomst bijdrage te kunnen leveren aan de digitale samenleving
items.raw_text: Om waarde te kunnen blijven toevoegen aan de digitale samenleving heeft Stichting ECP haar governance structuur aangepast. Eerder meldde Stichting ECP al dat ze de aanpassing aan het eind van dit jaar wil hebben ingericht, als uitkomst van een traject dat in 2024 in gang is gezet. Stichting ECP is er van overtuigd met deze governance structuur ook in de toekomst haar bijdrage te kunnen leveren via haar activiteiten en in samenwerking met het brede netwerk van publieke en private partijen die zich hiervoor inzetten. Een overzicht van wijzigingen governance en inrichting Stichting ECP is aan het einde van dit bericht opgenomen. items.title: Building Leadership Through Associations: A Conversation with Loida Garcia-Febo
items.raw_text: How can library associations strengthen leadership and help library and information professionals respond to increasingly complex and uncertain environments? On 25 June 2026, Loida Garcia-Febo, Chair of the IFLA Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS) , joined a conversation with Roxana Huaman Huriarte, Chair of the IFLA Latin America and the Caribbean Regional Division , and Nick Boxem, Chair of the IFLA Europe Regional Division , both members of the IFLA Regional Council leadership group. The conversation explored leadership within IFLA and library associations, and how strategic planning, capacity building and professional networks can help organisations and individuals respond more effectively to change. Leadership is a capacity that can be developed Leadership is not simply linked to holding a formal position but it is a capacity that can be intentionally developed through experience, training, mentoring, coaching and opportunities to work with others. For library associations, this means creating environments where current and emerging leaders can learn, test ideas, build confidence and develop the skills required to guide organisations through change. Garcia-Febo highlighted the importance of leadership training, mentoring and coaching, alongside team building and effective communication. items.title: Construyendo liderazgo a través de las asociaciones: Una conversación con Loida Garcia-Febo
items.raw_text: ¿Cómo pueden las asociaciones bibliotecarias fortalecer el liderazgo y ayudar a los bibliotecarios y profesionales de la información a responder a entornos cada vez más complejos e inciertos? El 25 de junio de 2026, Loida Garcia-Febo, Chair de la Sección de Gestión de Asociaciones de Bibliotecarios de IFLA (MLAS) , participó en una conversación con Roxana Huaman Huriarte, Chair de la División Regional de América Latina y el Caribe de IFLA , y Nick Boxem, Chair de la División Regional de Europa de IFLA , ambos miembros del grupo de liderazgo del Consejo Regional de IFLA. La conversación exploró el liderazgo dentro de IFLA y de las asociaciones bibliotecarias, así como la manera en que la planificación estratégica, el fortalecimiento de capacidades y las redes profesionales pueden ayudar a las organizaciones y a las personas a responder de manera más efectiva al cambio. El liderazgo es una capacidad que puede desarrollarse El liderazgo no está simplemente vinculado a ocupar una posición formal, sino que es una capacidad que puede desarrollarse intencionalmente a través de la experiencia, la formación, la mentoría, el coaching y las oportunidades para trabajar con otros. items.title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
items.raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. On the other hand, if stocks crash, ALA’s portfolio will not take as big a hit as it would have. About the funds The Association has about 70 different endowment funds that support d

items.title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.title: Hold the Phone
items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . And as more schools across the country enact phone-free policies—29 states and the District of Columbia have instituted bell-to-bell phone-free policies so far—many school libraries are experiencing a surge in popularity. items.title: Mall Wonder
items.raw_text: After serving its community for nearly 45 years in the same building, Escondido (Calif.) Public Library closed in April 2025 for an $11.6 million renovation. It was important to us, as the city’s lone library, to preserve access during construction. So one month later, our library opened a temporary location in a very different kind of facility: the nearby North County Mall, where services and collections were spread across six storefronts, including a former Abercrombie & Fitch clothing store. Of course, moving a library takes more than a month. Our planning took more than a year and required staff to work under tight deadlines, limited budgets, and high expectations. Here’s how we did it, and what we learned from the process. Choosing a location. It’s essential to consider whether the new location will match, improve upon, or limit access. Retailers and mall operators have already studied traffic patterns, visibility, parking, and nearby amenities. Leverage that knowledge to evaluate access. In our case, the public benefited from a highway and bus stop near the mall, and adjacency to a city park. The arrangement also gave the mall a stable civic tenant and created natural cross-traffic between library patrons and shoppers. The mall was not just available space; it was a location where public access, economic development, and community visibility could overlap. items.title: Dismantling Disinformation
items.raw_text: Library workers are well aware of the effects of book bans and censorship. Propaganda and disinformation are the flipside of the same coin. Understanding the complex relationships among these interrelated processes is more critical than ever, especially as libraries explore possible solutions and responses. The following books show how disinformation can lead to censorship and how censorship can, in turn, allow disinformation to thrive. Book Bans, Disinformation, and Cultural Erasure: The Censor­ship Movement in Libraries, Schools, and Society By Paul T. Jaeger Jaeger situates the current book-banning movement within a larger social and political effort to erase marginalized communities and culture. He provides clear definitions and examples of these processes and goals, including the roles played by technological progress and economic inequity. With accessible references (like the Beatles, Dungeons & Dragons, and Holmes and Watson) and nuanced examinations of McCarthyism, the history of libraries, and the myth of neutrality, this is a recommended read for anyone interested in a more expansive understanding of current First Amendment challenges. items.raw_text: When it comes to building resilient and equitable communities, libraries are natural leaders. We provide places where neighbors meet, learn, and support one another; where sustainability education becomes action; and where residents can find year-round climate refuge. When communities are resilient, they are better able to overcome barriers. The Obama Presidential Center (OPC) branch of Chicago Public Library (CPL) is an example of a library that strengthens the social infrastructure that underpins resilience. CPL Commissioner Chris Brown describes the branch as a civic platform for residents, artists, educators, and organizations to cocreate the life of the library and its surrounding public spaces. Though just 5,000 square feet, OPC was designed to spark connection, invite conversation, and inspire activities that encourage ­socialization and enjoyment. The branch partners with such nonprofits as the Art Institute of Chicago, the literary arts group StoryStudio Chicago , and the artist-led alt_Chicago . OPC is a striking example of how libraries do not just serve resilient communities, they help create them. On the Gulf Coast, sustainability is a daily requirement. Reed Purdue University Libraries Greenley Goedde Creech Purdue University Libraries Source College & Research Libraries Vol 87, No 5 (2026) Vol 87, No 5 (2026) Abstract The goal of this bibliometric study was to explore the broader publication patterns of academic librarians in both information and library science (ISLS) and interdisciplinary research for the years 2009 to 2023. Web of Science data were collected for 12 academic libraries. The results showed that while the number of ISLS publications has dropped, interdisciplinary publications have increased dramatically with a broad range of disciplines represented, and that collaborations in the medical sciences were a major contributor to this increase. items.title: Disclosing AI Use in Academic Research, a New Global Study From Oxford University Press
items.raw_text: Published today by Oxford University Press (OUP): We have updated our author and editor guidelines on the responsible, appropriate, and transparent use of AI, including a policy outlining what AI use should be disclosed when preparing manuscripts for our journals. In a recent global survey of more than 2,600 researchers, nearly three-quarters (74%) of respondents revealed they were unclear what AI use they should disclose, despite there being strong support for disclosure. With 44% of researchers concerned that disclosing their use of AI will negatively impact how others view their work, and only 36% recording their AI use during their research, our survey emphasizes the growing gap between AI use and disclosure in academic research, and recognizes the need for clear disclosure policies. Many (68%) agree that AI tools can reduce accessibility barriers, too. The report also shows a widening gap between libraries moving beyond experimentation with AI and those still in the earliest stages of AI adoption. 51% of libraries in active implementation operate under joint library and IT governance, against 26% of the sample overall, signaling the importance of structured governance models and interdepartmental collaboration. items.title: Digital Preservation: Internet Archive Releases Online Archive (199,000 Articles) of BET Journalism No Longer Available on the Live Web
items.raw_text: From the Internet Archive (via Bluesky, X, and Mastodon): Much of BET’s digital journalism is no longer available on the live web. Internet Archive has preserved more than 199,000 BET articles over the years. They can now be accessed through The Wayback Machine & a new pilot explorer: https:// wayback-labs.sf.archive.org/bet-explorer/ Background From Huff Post: Black Entertainment Television, more commonly known as BET, has removed all digital articles from its website in a push to prioritize video content, HuffPost’s Phil Lewis reported Friday. Multimedia reporting remains on the site and BET’s social channels. However, the move to erase the written content came without warning, leaving many writers with no trace of their work, Lewis reported. “Years of news articles are now gone forever,” he wrote. items.title: New Freckle Project Report Examines 15 Years of Public Library Use
items.raw_text: From EveryLibrary Institute: A new Freckle Project Report, “15 Years of IMLS Figures” , looks at national public library statistics from 2010 through 2024 and identifies a striking contrast: American public libraries have more facilities, more staff, and higher levels of funding than at any point in the period examined, while several major measures of physical library use remain substantially below their 2010 levels. The Freckle Project is led by researcher Tim Coates, and its publication is supported by the EveryLibrary Institute. The August 2026 Report examines 15 years of data from the Institute of Museum and Library Services on America’s public libraries. In 2024, the United States had 17,580 public library facilities and 147,289 library employees, while public libraries received nearly $18 billion for operations and another $1.6 billion for capital expenditures. Yet annual visits declined from approximately 1.57 billion in 2010 to 869 million in 2024, while total circulation fell from approximately 2.47 billion to 1.71 billion. Coates’s analysis highlights an especially significant decline in adult physical circulation. After subtracting electronic and children’s circulation from total circulation, he estimates that this category fell approximately 68 percent between 2010 and 2024. items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. Instead, I left with a notebook full of starred ideas, half-written thoughts, and questions scribbled in the margins. Looking back, those messy notes reveal the sessions that stayed with me long after the conference ended. Conversations about internal communication, programming for older adults, and flexible, community-centered services challenged my assumptions and sparked new ideas for my own work. Sessions including “Becoming One Library: How to Build Better Internal Communications,” “Aging Together: Library Programming for Older Adults,” and “Memory Cafes in Libraries: Creating Meaningful Connections” reframed how I think about serving both staff and patrons. Ideas I Starred One of the most memorable concepts came from “Becoming One Library: How to Build Better Internal Communications.” Mary Kapusta described how her library system developed clearer, more intentional communication practices, including a framework called “Skim, Swim, Dive.” The model structures communication so staff can quickly identify key information and then choose how deeply they engage based on their needs and available time. The idea resonated with me because it recognizes a reality every workplace faces: staff absorb information differently, have varying capacities, and don’t need every message delivered in the same format. items.title: Building More Inclusive Libraries for Patrons with Disabilities
items.raw_text: At every conference I attend, I hope to leave with at least one idea I can realistically adapt and implement at my own library. At PLA 2026, I found that inspiration in my very first session: *”Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities.”* Presenter Courtney Walker, founder of Libraries for All, shared how her experience as a school librarian led her to rethink traditional picture book collections for students with disabilities. She noticed that many students were not engaging with standard picture books, often returning them unread or damaged. In some cases, families stopped checking out books altogether. Seeking a solution, Walker adapted a resource commonly used in classrooms: laminated books enhanced with sensory and interactive elements. By modifying these materials for library use and creating durable books with touch-and-feel components, she found that students with disabilities engaged more actively with stories and enjoyed more positive and equitable reading experiences. Walker now works as a consultant through Libraries for All and collaborated with fellow presenters Janet Cox and Maggie Fox of Plano Public Library (PPL) in Texas to develop a full collection of adapted books. Their team selected popular picture books, organized volunteer workshops to create adapted versions, trained staff to support the collection, and developed cataloging practices for these unique materials. items.title: Information Strategies for Libraries in the Age of AI
items.raw_text: Librarians must actively adapt to an information landscape increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI), search engine optimization (SEO), and algorithm-driven content. During the PLA 2026 session, *”Trust & Verify: Information Accuracy in the Age of SEO, AI, and Algorithms,”* Nathaniel Burnard, Systems Services Manager at Allen County Public Library, offered a practical and timely examination of how these forces influence the way we, and our patrons, discover and evaluate information. As a 2026 PLA scholarship recipient, I had the opportunity to attend Burnard’s insightful presentation in Minneapolis. Burnard began by explaining the differences between misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation (MDM). While these terms are often used interchangeably, they differ based on the intent behind the creation or sharing of information. Misinformation is false or inaccurate information shared without intent to deceive. Disinformation is deliberately false information created to manipulate, mislead, or cause harm. Malinformation contains truthful information that is presented in a misleading, sensationalized, or harmful way. To help identify MDM, Burnard encouraged attendees to ask critical questions such as, “Does this content provoke a strong emotional response?” and “Does it use small pieces of valid information that have been exaggerated or distorted?” He also emphasized the importance of avoiding engagement with misleading content. items.title: One Year Later: The Digital Equity Act Cancellation and Libraries
items.raw_text: May 8, 2026, marked the one-year anniversary of the Trump Administration’s cancellation of the Digital Equity Act (DEA). The $2.75 billion Digital Equity Act was a part of a coordinated effort to provide communities across the U.S. with high-speed broadband and the skills and technology needed to thrive in our increasingly digital world. Libraries and other community anchor institutions were integral to the planning of this once-in-a-generation opportunity to address the digital divide. Collectively, these groups spent precious resources and staff time applying for DEA program grants, leading related coalition building efforts, and conducting outreach and asset mapping. The abrupt cancellation of the DEA grants last year was a significant blow to digital inclusion programs nationwide, impacting millions of Americans. According to the Idaho Commission for Libraries , over 80% of the state’s DEA Capacity Grant award “was slated for subgrants supporting rural Idahoans, including older adults and veterans.” Public and tribal libraries across the state would have benefited from grants to replace outdated computers to offer public training on cybersecurity and technology use. In Maine, nearly 130,000 people would have been directly served by DEA-funded programs, such as digital skills training, technical support, telehealth access, and affordable device programs. items.title: Rennie McDougall On How Social And Historical Forces Molded Twentieth Century Dance
items.raw_text: Rennie McDougall ‘s Nonstop Bodies: How Dance Shaped New York City gives readers a thrilling new perspective on twentieth century New York City by investigating the different choreographers, dancers, and dance movements that flourished there during that time. McDougall guides the reader through various dance movements, from the marathon dances of the Prohibition era to the Lindy Hop to the Rockettes and beyond. All the while, he catalogues the dense web of lineages that developed among specific dances and artists, allowing readers to see relationships among disparate dance forms that might not be immediately apparent. McDougall also dives into how social and historical forces directly molded the evolving dance forms, and the unique position New York City held to create countless connections between dancers and choreographers not only in the moment, but across time as well. Critics have heaped praise on the book, with Library Journal hailing it as “a love song to dance in all its forms and the city that invented and perfected so many styles.” McDougall spoke with us about taking a different approach to dance history, bringing readers into the immediacy of dancing, and how the texture of the dancers’ lives unconsciously affected the evolution of dance.
